TI Design and validation: CODES questionnaire on the teaching in higher
   education
SO ALTERIDAD-REVISTA DE EDUCACION
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE university teaching; questionnaire; higher education; pedagogy; labor
   conditions; digital teaching skills
ID SCALE
AB This study is part of a broader research project on university admission, retention, and virtualization in public universities. Its aim is to present the design and preliminary validation of the Questionnaire on the Teaching Profession in Higher Education (CODES), an instrument that operationalizes the teaching profession through three dimensions: pedagogical practices, organizational setting, and the use of digital technologies. CODES was developed as an online questionnaire using five-point Likert-type response scales and is currently in a preliminary stage of psychometric development. Content validity was assessed through expert judgment involving 15 specialists, and Aiken's V coefficient was calculated for each item, yielding values ranging from 0.96 to 1.00. The pilot study included the voluntary participation of 66 faculty members from 11 academic units at a public university in central Argentina. High levels of internal consistency were obtained, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.87 and a McDonald's omega of 0.91 for the overall construct. The proposed dimensional structure was supported by a preliminary exploratory factor analysis (EFA), although confirmatory factor analyses have not yet been conducted. CODES constitutes a contextualized and relevant instrument for studying the teaching profession and is sensitive to transformations in teaching practices. Its preliminary psychometric properties support its use in future research and guide subsequent validation stages, including confirmatory factor analyses with larger samples.

TI Didactic communication: a case study in two spanish universities
SO ALTERIDAD-REVISTA DE EDUCACION
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE communication; higher education; learning; life skills; didactic;
   educational practice
ID FEEDBACK; TEACHERS
AB The integration of emotion, motivation, language, and thought into training processes in Higher Education is a key factor that fosters the comprehensive development of students. The main objective of this research work is to analyze didactic communication as a tool that influences the development of the cognitive, emotional, and professional capacities of university students, based on the experiences and perceptions of the teaching staff. A qualitative research methodology is employed through the biographical-narrative method, and the AQUAD 7 software program is used for data analysis. The results show that university professors consider didactic communication as a comprehensive training tool that promotes emotions and activates students'thinking in their educational process at the university. Furthermore, didactic communication is not limited to the mere transmission of information, but rather favors the comprehensive development of cognitive, emotional, and social capacities. This study concludes that university didactic communication must be integrated from an educational practice that stimulates the personal and affective dimensions of students to achieve quality learning in Higher Education. In this way, it is evidenced that didactic communication constitutes the tool par excellence for successful university interaction.

TI Gamification and collaborative learning in higher education students
SO ALTERIDAD-REVISTA DE EDUCACION
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE collaborative learning; gamification; instructional design; higher
   education; students; methodology
ID PERCEPTIONS
AB This study was conducted to determine whether gamification strategies influence student collaboration in a higher education course and to establish how these strategies affect students' collaborative learning. To achieve this, a blended learning course was designed for an official Mexican program using gamification strategies. A total of 128 students participated, divided into four large groups. They were administered the COLLES survey at the beginning and end of the course. Key informants were also interviewed to gain deeper insight into their perceptions of the course and the collaborative learning achieved. The results revealed that scores across all dimensions of the COLLES increased from the pretest to the post-test. Meanwhile, the interviews identified seven themes that align with the analyzed dimensions. To achieve these results, three key elements were identified: first, ensuring that the course design is appropriate; second, ensuring student commitment to teamwork; and third, the instructor's support for students to enable collaborative learning. Among the findings is that gamification strategies do have an impact on group work, particularly in terms of relevance and reflective thinking; furthermore, the three key elements mentioned above were essential for fostering collaborative learning.

TI Good practices in the organization of inclusive support in schools
SO ALTERIDAD-REVISTA DE EDUCACION
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE inclusive education; inclusive supports; educational innovation;
   co-teaching; active methodologies; primary education
ID EDUCATION; STUDENTS; VOICES
AB Inclusive support systems are a cornerstone of schools, capable of driving substantial and far-reaching changes in educational policies, cultures and practices. The overall aim of this study is to analyse good practices in the organisation of educational support systems that promote the inclusion of all pupils in mainstream primary school classrooms, based on the views of the educational community. This research is conducted using an inductive qualitative approach. A total of 329 professionals involved in the organisation of educational support systems across 25 primary schools participated in the study. Semi-structured interviews were used to gather the data. A qualitative content analysis was carried out using ATLAS.ti 25 software. The results show that the effective organisation of inclusive support systems requires clear planning that defines inclusion within the school, based on a comprehensive analysis of existing barriers. The need for mainstream and support staff to plan jointly, based on agreed improvement objectives, is highlighted. Furthermore, the practices proposed by the professionals include the creation of intervention protocols to address the identified barriers, co-teaching, curriculum prioritisation, flexible grouping and active methodologies, which are considered essential for optimising the organisation and functioning of educational support systems in the schools analysed.

   inclusion
SO ALTERIDAD-REVISTA DE EDUCACION
LA Spanish
DT Article

   Psychopathology
AB The current educational landscape supports an inclusive treatment of the diversities present in society. Issues related to hearing and language disorders are highlighted, that Psychopathology offers a response. These situations are represented through the imagery of visual culture. The present work aims to analyze language pathologies in Disney classic films, from a socio-educational position and paradigm to raise awareness about an inclusive treatment of these diversities in classrooms. Overall, conclusions are reached to a didactic use of Disney animated feature films to make visible and inclusively address issues related to linguistic diversity.

TI Construction and application of a crowdsourcing-based model for digital
   textbooks in higher education
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital textbooks; Crowdsourcing; Generative artificial intelligence;
   Model construction
ID STUDENT; DESIGN; IMPACT
AB Digitalization of textbooks constitutes a pivotal aspect of the digital transformation of education, playing an indispensable role in the development of a modern education system. Currently, the construction of digital textbooks in higher education lacks a shareable and reusable model. Crowdsourcing is an innovative concept that leverages collective wisdom to improve the quality of resources, transcending organizational boundaries and facilitating the flow of knowledge. This study adopts the design-based research paradigm and comprehensively applies a variety of research methods to construct and implement a crowdsourcing-based construction model for digital textbooks in higher education. The model includes a knowledge subsystem, a process subsystem, and an organizational subsystem, covering crowdsourcing participants such as professionals, ordinary participants and artificial intelligence. The digital textbook developed based on this framework has demonstrated significant user satisfaction in terms of content, teaching, technical design, evaluation, opportunities for deep learning, accessibility, and security. It is expected that the construction model of the digital textbooks in high education built in this study can further enrich the research outcomes of digital textbooks, and provide a model reference for digital textbook construction in higher education.

TI Construction of a collaborative learning grouping model: Integration of
   knowledge complementarity and dynamic diagnosis
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Collaborative learning; Knowledge mastery state diagnosis; Collaborative
   learning grouping model
AB In the process of collaborative learning, effective grouping is the key to improving learning efficiency. A well-structured collaborative learning group can markedly improve the learning efficiency of both individuals and the group as a whole. Nonetheless, current grouping methods for collaborative learning frequently fall short of a comprehensive assessment of students' knowledge proficiency, thereby failing to guarantee that group members' knowledge structures are mutually complementary. Therefore, a grouping model combining knowledge complementarity and dynamic diagnosis is proposed. The grouping model is divided into five layers. Firstly, the learning objective analysis layer deconstructs the teaching content into several core knowledge points. On this basis, the dynamic knowledge diagnosis layer uses the improved deep knowledge tracking model DKVMN-KT to dynamically diagnose students' mastery of core knowledge points. Then, in the personalized grouping layer, K-means algorithm is used to cluster the personalized grouping results. Furthermore, teachers were involved in the manual fine-tuning of the grouping results. Finally, the model forms a closed-loop feedback link through a deep interactive optimization layer to promote the iterative optimization of the collaborative learning grouping model. The experimental results indicate that the collaborative learning grouping model is helpful to effectively group students at the level of knowledge structure, and can improve the efficiency of collaborative learning, In order to guarantee more equitable and diverse grouping outcomes, this methodology promotes positive interplay among students, enabling them to mutually learn from one another and thereby enhance their comprehension of diverse knowledge points effectively.

TI Generative AI and education: Exploring the interplay between teachers'
   epistemic beliefs and self-regulated learning
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Epistemic beliefs; Self-regulated learning; Generative AI; Structural
   model
ID EPISTEMOLOGICAL BELIEFS; PERSONAL EPISTEMOLOGY; COGNITION
AB The rapid advancement of generative AI (GenAI) technologies, such as ChatGPT, has significantly transformed the educational landscape. Previous research highlights the impact of teachers' beliefs on their professional development and instructional methods. There is a growing need to align teachers' beliefs with the latest technological advancements. This study investigates the relationships between teachers' epistemic beliefs and their self-regulated learning under GenAI contexts. With a sample of 687 educators, this research employs exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses to validate the GenAI Epistemic Beliefs Questionnaire and the GenAI Self-regulated Learning Questionnaire. Structural equation modeling reveals that specific dimensions of GenAI epistemic beliefs, particularly the justification for GenAI-generated content and the structure of GenAI-generated content, significantly influence the planning phase of self-regulated learning. Teachers with sophisticated beliefs in justifying GenAI-generated content demonstrate more effective planning strategies. In contrast, those with structured beliefs in GenAI-generated content exhibit a more rigid approach to planning. However, these epistemic beliefs do not directly impact the adaptation phase of self-regulated learning; instead, planning serves as a full mediator, emphasizing the critical role of initial self-regulated learning planning in fostering adaptability. This study underscores the importance of understanding how educators' beliefs about GenAI influence their self-regulated learning.

TI Revisiting online learning readiness: Scale development and insights
   from Taiwanese elementary school students
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE 21st century skills/thinking skills; Distance education and online
   learning; K-12 education; Teacher training
ID PERCEPTION; SIZE
AB This study developed and validated a scale for assessing online learning readiness among students aged 10 to 12 years in grades 4 to 6. The scale is called the Online Learning Readiness Scale for Elementary School (OLRS-E). To establish the reliability and validity of the scale, expert insights were gathered using the fuzzy Delphi method, and exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were conducted on separate samples of 152 and 423 students, respectively. The OLRS-E comprises four key dimensions. Self-directed learning measures students' motivation and ability to regulate their own learning behaviors. Communication self-efficacy assesses students' confidence in expressing themselves and interacting in online environments. Family support captures the practical and emotional assistance students receive from caregivers during online learning. Technical support reflects students' perceived competence in using digital tools and resolving basic technological issues. Among these, technical support yielded the highest score, indicating a high degree of technological readiness among Taiwanese elementary school students, followed by family support and communication self-efficacy. By contrast, self-directed learning yielded the lowest score, indicating a lower degree of self-directed learning readiness among these students. Overall, these findings of student readiness have major implications for parents and teachers regarding online learning efficacy.

TI Exploring the relationship between student engagement and use of blended
   MOOCs: A developing nation's STEM students' perspective
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Revised community of inquiry; Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of
   Technology; Blended MOOCs; Student engagement; University STEM students
ID INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; CONTINUANCE INTENTION; PERCEIVED USEFULNESS;
   LEARNING PRESENCE; SELF-REGULATION; UNIFIED THEORY; ACCEPTANCE; ONLINE;
   INQUIRY; COMMUNITY
AB Massive open online courses (MOOCs) can disseminate academic knowledge, such as complete courses, to students and lifelong learners from all backgrounds and anywhere. Using a quantitative approach, this study examines the relationship between engagement, acceptance, and use of blended MOOCs among 1875 STEM students at the University of Cape Coast (UCC), Ghana. The theoretical basis is the proposed revised Community of Inquiry (RCoI) framework and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). A structured questionnaire was designed and distributed via Google Forms to a randomly selected sample of 3,506 students using a two-stage cluster sampling technique. The survey achieved an 82% response rate, with 2,875 participants completing it. Out of these 2,875 participants, 1,875 were STEM students, and they were explicitly used for this paper. Structural equation modelling was employed to analyse how the RCoI model-encompassing cognitive, social, teaching, and learning presences-affects students' acceptance and use of blended MOOCs. According to the study, STEM students' engagement significantly impacts their ability to utilise blended MOOCs. The findings showed that within blended MOOCs, the presence of RCoI had a significant positive relationship with STEM students' engagement. Again, the findings reveal significant influences of STEM students' engagement on performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions, highlighting the need for administrative and technical support to enhance the effective adoption of blended MOOCs. This study contributes robust insights into the dynamics of student interaction and learning outcomes in blended learning environments such as blended MOOCs within developing countries.

TI A systematic literature review: Game design elements in
   constructivistserious game
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational technology; Constructivism; Game design element; Active
   learning; Conceptualization
ID SERIOUS GAME; VIDEO GAME; FLOW
AB Serious games are recognized for promoting knowledge and skill transfer through active learning aligned with constructivist principles. However, the availability of guidelines on how specific game design elements align with these principles are limited. This study conducted a systematic literature review using Web of Science and ScienceDirect, analyzing 39 selected studies to profile trends in constructivist-serious games and identifying aligned GDEs. Findings showed that most studies focused on STEM subjects, targeted university students, used quantitative methods, and favored computer-based platforms. The most commonly applied theories were situated learning and problem-based learning. The most frequently used and strongly supported GDEs were "imposed choices", "sensations", and "objectives". This highlights the importance of learners' autonomy and clear educational objectives within an authentic learning environment in designing a constructivist-serious game. Each element was evaluated against four constructivist factors: interaction, problem-solving, active learning, and discovery, resulting in a conceptual mapping of GDEs to constructivist learning. These findings provide practical guidance for integrating constructivist principles into serious game design.

TI Classroom analytics with educational big data: A comparative approach
   for sustainable teacher reflection
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Classroom analytics; Classroom engagement; Educational big data;
   Comparative analysis; Teacher reflection
ID LEARNING ANALYTICS; CHALLENGES; STUDENTS
AB This study investigates the use of educational big data to support classroom analytics, focusing on extracting comparable classroom datasets to enhance teacher reflection. We developed methods to automatically identify and analyze comparable classroom datasets based on student interactions with digital learning materials using log data. Through two analyses, we examined the effectiveness of cosine similarity, the radial basis function (RBF) kernel, and the Jaccard coefficient for identifying comparable classes. Additionally, Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) was used to evaluate classroom engagement patterns. Our results indicate that cosine similarity and the RBF kernel are effective for detecting similarities in classroom data, while the Jaccard coefficient is less dependable. The classroom engagement analysis showed significant differences in engagement patterns across specific classes, offering opportunities for teachers to reflect on and improve their teaching practices. This approach offers a scalable way to gather data and feedback continuously, encouraging ongoing reflections on teaching strategies. Future research should apply these methods in various educational environments to validate their effectiveness.

TI Influencing factors of adult assessors' online assessment behavioral
   performance: A moderated mediation model
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Assessing peers; Behavioral control; Peer assessment; Subjective norm;
   Theory of planned behavior
ID PEER ASSESSMENT; TECHNOLOGY
AB The study aimed to examine the moderated mediation model for the influencing factors of adult assessors' behavioral performance in online assessment (OA). The participants included 200 graduate students from a university seminar course utilizing an OA system. The results indicate that OA continuance intention fully mediates the relationships between the three antecedents (i.e., OA attitude, OA subjective norm, and perceived OA behavioral control) and OA behavioral performance. OA experience positively moderates the relationship between OA continuance intention and OA behavioral performance, and further moderates the mediating effect of OA continuance intention between OA attitude and OA behavioral performance, indicating a moderated mediation effect. This study expands the perspective and applicability of the theory of planned behavior (TPB) and provides practical implications for online peer assessment.

TI Examining the effects of generative AI chatbots on EFL learners'
   listening and speaking skills and the perceived usefulness
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI); Chatbots; Listening ability;
   Speaking ability; EFL (English as a Foreign Language) learners
ID INTELLIGENT PERSONAL ASSISTANTS; 2ND-LANGUAGE; WILLINGNESS; L2;
   COMPREHENSION; NEGOTIATION; COMMUNICATE
AB The use of chatbots has attracted much attention because it can create interactive and immersive learning environments for EFL (English as a Foreign Language) learners. While learners benefit from interactions with chatbots, they indicate that chatbots still have limitations in understanding their intent and expressions to maintain natural conversations. To provide learners better experiences, our team created the CoolE Bot based on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), which helps improve the bot's communication capabilities. This study investigated the effects of CoolE Bot on EFL learners' listening and speaking skills, as well as its perceived usefulness across two proficiency levels. It adopted a pre-and post-test design involving 42 students. They took listening and speaking tests, engaged with CoolE Bot for seven weeks, and completed a survey. Statistical analysis indicated that, while both high-and low-proficiency groups showed significant improvements in speaking skill, the improvements in listening skill were less pronounced and did not reach statistical significance. In terms of perceived usefulness, the low-proficiency group found CoolE Bot more beneficial than their high-proficiency peers across several aspects, including different language skills development and increased opportunities for speaking practice. These results suggest that CoolE Bot is a valuable tool for enhancing speaking skills and supporting listening development.

TI Guest editorial: Robotics facilitated teaching and learning: An embodied
   cognition and multimodal perspective
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creativity; Educational robots; Embodied cognition; Multimodality;
   Human-robot interaction
AB This special issue examines the landscape of robotics-facilitated teaching and learning through the theoretical lenses of embodied cognition and multimodal perspectives. The ten selected papers evidently report how both physical and virtual robots foster meaningful learning through social presence, multisensory interaction, pedagogical integration, and adaptive feedback. Collectively, these studies underscore the efficacy of synergizing robotic technologies with complementary pedagogical strands, ranging from scaffolding strategies (such as digital storytelling, concept mapping, and gamification) to collaborative and embodied processes (including socially shared regulation of learning and multimodal interaction), while also incorporating dialectic and inquiry-driven methods (such as Socratic dialogue and productive failure). Furthermore, the contributing insights reveal that well-orchestrated human-robot interaction yields multifaceted benefits across diverse age groups and subject domains, concurrently enhancing students' cognitive faculties (e.g., computational thinking, critical problem-solving, and creativity) and non-cognitive growth (e.g., empathy, socio-emotional learning, and professional identity).

TI Investigating the effectiveness of artificial intelligence-powered
   robots in learning medical English: A mixed-methods study on
   sociolinguistic competence and perceptions
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Adaptive learning; Artificial intelligence; Medical English; Robots;
   Sociolinguistic competence
ID LANGUAGE; EDUCATION; CHATGPT; TRENDS
AB Recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence-powered robots have introduced a variety of educational technologies aimed at accommodating standard varieties of languages. However, the adaptiveness of the knowledge bases of these robots in establishing adaptive language learning at universities remains underexplored. This quasi-experimental study involved 1041 students from 13 academic disciplines with diverse first languages. Utilizing a parallel design, while students in the control group learned medical English skills through non-adaptive AI-powered robots, students in the experimental group learned the same skills through adaptive AI-powered robots. We assessed the effectiveness of learning medical English through Artificial Intelligence-powered robots with(out) adaptive knowledge bases, employing Objective Structured Video Exams for formative assessment. Additionally, the participants shared their perceptions of Artificial Intelligence-powered robots in medical English education through semi-structured interviews. Quantitative findings indicated that students using adaptive Artificial Intelligence-powered robots showed a greater sociolinguistic competence in medical English compared to those learning with non-adaptive robots. The qualitative findings suggested that the students in disciplines requiring direct interaction with patients and healthcare staff expressed a more positive perception of learning medical English through Artificial Intelligence-powered robots. While both groups acknowledged the value of the course, those engaging with adaptive systems demonstrated a great appreciation for the learning process and outcomes. Based on these results, we offer recommendations for researchers on effectively integrating Artificial Intelligence-powered robots into university language education, highlighting the potential for enhanced learning experiences through adaptive technologies.

TI Effects of robot tutor and peer roles on preschoolers' empathy,
   anthropomorphism perceptions, learning behaviors, and teacher
   reflections
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Robot; Preschooler; Empathy; Social learning theory; Human-robot
   interaction; Behavior patterns
AB In the age of artificial intelligence, empathy is crucial for preschoolers' social adaptation and personal development. The development of Humanoid Intelligent Robots (HIRs) offers an opportunity to provide preschoolers with personalized interactive experiences. This study recruited 77 rural preschoolers aged 5 to 6 years as participants, who were randomly assigned to an R-tutor group, an R-peer group, and a conventional teaching group. An 8-week empathy course was conducted to explore the impact of different roles of HIRs on their empathy. The results of the questionnaire analysis showed that the R-tutor method improved preschoolers' empathy more than the R-peer method and the conventional teaching method; the R-peer method did not enhance preschoolers' empathy compared to the conventional teaching method. In addition, perceptions of robot anthropomorphism in the R-tutor group were significantly higher than those in the conventional teaching group. Behavior analysis results showed that the R-tutor group significantly outperformed the R-peer group and the conventional teaching group in terms of emotional empathy and behavioral empathy, while the interactions in the R-peer group and the conventional teaching group remained mainly at the level of cognitive empathy. The teacher's teaching reflections indicated that robot tutors can stimulate preschoolers' interest in learning, optimize their emotional experiences, and develop their empathy. The Situation-Cognition-Emotion-Behavior (SCEB) empathy learning model proposed in this study provides a theoretical framework for cultivating preschoolers' empathy. Furthermore, the exploration of using HIRs with different roles to foster preschoolers' empathy also offers valuable practical experience for preschool teachers in conducting empathy education.

TI From collaboration to cognition: The effects of a gamified
   robot-assisted social shared regulated learning approach on students'
   learning outcomes in STEM
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Social shared regulated learning; Robotics-Facilitated Teaching;
   Gamification; Creative thinking
ID SEQUENTIAL PATTERNS; SELF; CONTEXT
AB Previous studies have shown that Social Shared Regulated Learning (SSRL) can facilitate knowledge construction and collaborative learning in STEM courses. Robots, as learning partners, play a crucial role in supporting SSRL processes and promoting collaboration. In addition, the game elements in gamification can effectively stimulate students' learning motivation, promote changes in student behavior, and improve learning outcomes. Based on this, this study proposed a gamified robot-assisted SSRL approach and evaluated its effectiveness in terms of improving students' academic performance, learning motivation and higher-order thinking through a quasi-experiment. The experimental group (n = 30) used a gamified robot-assisted SSRL approach (GR-SSRL), while the control group (n = 27) used a conventional robot-assisted SSRL approach (R-SSRL). The research results showed that the GR-SSRL approach can effectively improve students' academic performance and external learning motivation, and can significantly improve the creative thinking ability of students with low collaboration ability. This study shows that the integration of certain learning tools can effectively support SSRL, and indicate that the combination of a variety of technical means can produce synergistic effects to improve learning outcomes.

TI Time sequence-oriented concept mapping-supported robot storytelling:
   Enhancing high school students' learning performance and perceptions in
   health education
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Time sequence-oriented concept map (TSCM); Robot-based digital
   storytelling; Cancer-preventing diet; Higher-order thinking; Critical
   thinking
ID ACHIEVEMENT; MOTIVATION; THINKING; MAPS
AB Cancer incidence has been rising among younger populations, making it increasingly important to educate adolescents about the relationship between diet and chronic diseases. However, conventional teaching methods often fail to promote deep and self-directed learning. Robot-based digital storytelling offers an engaging approach, but research shows that without effective scaffolding, students may struggle to construct coherent, knowledge-rich narratives. This study proposes a time sequence-oriented concept mapping approach to support high school students in designing robot storytelling projects focused on cancer-preventing dietary knowledge. A quasi-experimental design was adopted, with 19 students in the experimental group using time sequence-oriented concept mapping for robot-based digital storytelling and 19 students in the control group following a conventional robot-based digital storytelling model. Results indicated that the time sequence-oriented concept mapping-supported group outperformed the control group in learning achievement, communication tendencies, collaborative learning, critical thinking, and group self-efficacy. Interview findings further highlighted the model's benefits in supporting knowledge construction and teamwork. This study provides empirical support for integrating time sequence-oriented concept mapping into robotics-supported health education.

TI Dialogues with AI agents in elementary student writing: Impacts on
   performance, behavior, and cognition
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-assisted writing; Critical thinking; AI agent; Student-AI dialogue;
   Cognitive scaffolding
ID CRITICAL THINKING SKILLS
AB As artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted writing tools are increasingly adopted, their impact on students' critical thinking (CT) skills has garnered attention. However, behavioral and cognitive differences among different CT students using AI-assisted writing tools remain underexplored. This study developed multimodal AI-assisted writing agent (AI-AWA) based on Socratic dialogue principles and grounded in sociocultural theory. It analyzed the student-AI conversation transcripts and essays of 45 elementary school students using repeated measures analysis of covariance and Epistemic Network Analysis. It is found that High-CT students outperformed Low-CT students in terms of academic achievement. High-CT students demonstrated more pronounced improvements in grammar, whereas Low-CT students exhibited greater gains in content and organization. In terms of behavioral patterns, the High-CT group frequently posed challenging questions and independently constructed their own outlines, while the Low-CT students exhibited an increase in reasoning behaviors and a reduction in AI dependency. With respect to cognitive patterns, the High-CT students maintained advanced cognitive engagement, while the Low-CT students showed gradual improvement. These findings highlight how students with different CT levels engage differently with the AI agents, suggesting its potential for supporting diverse writing and thinking strategies. This study suggests that heuristic AI tools need to be designed differentially, using open scaffolding for High-CT students to stimulate their deep thinking, and more structured cognitive scaffolding for Low-CT students to balance tool support with CT autonomy. Such strategies allow for the dynamic maintenance and cultivation of critical thinking alongside writing support.

TI Productive failure-based robot programming: Effects on primary school
   students' computational thinking, self-efficacy, growth mindset, and
   learning perceptions
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Productive failure; Robot programming; Computational thinking;
   Self-efficacy; Growth mindset
ID FRAMEWORK; DESIGN
AB Robot programming has become an effective means to promote primary school students' computational thinking (CT). Direct instruction (DI), characterized by teacher instruction followed by student problem-solving, is a commonly adopted teaching approach for robot programming and CT. However, by emphasizing task completion and minimizing failures, DI limits students' ability to understand the essence of problem-solving and learn from mistakes. In contrast, productive failure (PF) involves students' problem-solving followed by teacher instruction, treating failure as a valuable experience that fosters deeper learning and problem-solving skills. Hence, this research compared the effects of the productive failure-based robot programming (PF-RP) and direct instruction-based robot programming (DI-RP) approaches on primary school students' CT, self-efficacy, growth mindset, and learning perceptions. A quasi-experimental study involving both quantitative and qualitative data was designed. The sample comprised 87 third-grade students from China, with 43 students in the PF-RP group and 44 students in the DI-RP group. Results revealed that (1) both approaches enhanced students' CT, with the PF-RP approach demonstrating greater improvements than the DI-RP approach over time; (2) both approaches improved students' self-efficacy, but no significant differences were detected between the two approaches over time; (3) only the PF-RP approach significantly promoted students' growth mindset and showed greater improvements than the DI-RP approach over time; and (4) students perceived that the PF-RP approach is an effective teaching approach that helped them think of more solutions and strengthen their understanding.

TI Fostering pre-service teachers' social and emotional learning and
   professional identity through self-explanation-integrated CIDI-based
   GenAI digital storytelling
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Multi-agent; Pre-service teachers; Social-emotional competence;
   Professional identity; Self-explanation
ID CRITICAL METAPHOR ANALYSIS; HEALTH; COMPETENCE
AB The development of social and emotional learning (SEL) competence is vital for pre-service teachers' professional identity. Although generative AI (GenAI)-supported digital storytelling can promote this development, it may also induce cognitive load and technostress if not properly guided. Therefore, this study proposed a self-explanation-integrated CIDI (Clarify, Ideate, Develop, Implement) approach to facilitate SEL internalization and ease GenAI-related stress. It explored participants' perceptions of human-AI interaction through metaphor analysis and interviews. A total of 177 pre-service teachers were recruited for the study and assigned to either the S-CIDI (self-explanation-integrated CIDI) group (n = 90) or the C-CIDI (conventional CIDI) group (n = 87). Results showed that the S-CIDI model significantly improved learning performance and enhanced professional identity. Although social-emotional competence (SEC) improved in both groups, stress mindset increased across all conditions. Metaphor analysis and interviews revealed that the S-CIDI group exhibited weaker critical reflection on the AI-generated content, suggesting that caution is needed against the potential suppression of autonomous thinking by highly structured support. In metaphorical representations, both groups commonly described AI agents as "Assistants." The S-CIDI group preferred authoritative metaphors such as "Tutor," whereas the C-CIDI group tended to use metaphors like "Partner," emphasizing human-AI collaboration and co-creation concepts. The interviews further revealed that although both models promoted the development of social-emotional competence and professional identity, they showed differences in technology perception and agency construction, with the S-CIDI model potentially fostering over-reliance and diminishing critical autonomy.

TI Fostering primary school students' computational thinking with
   multimodal embodied interaction model in educational robotics courses: A
   design-based research
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Computational thinking; Educational robotics; Multimodal interaction;
   Embodied cognition; Design-based research (DBR)
ID EXPLORATION
AB Educational Robotics (ER) courses are widely acknowledged as an effective method for fostering K-12 students' Computational Thinking (CT). Previous teaching practices predominantly relied on unimodal visual instructional imitation and procedural task-based approaches. These approaches disconnect abstract computational symbols from embodied experiences and limit the in-depth development of students' CT. To address this challenge, the present study proposes and systematically validates the Multimodal Embodied Interaction (MEI) model through an integrated perspective that combines embodied cognition with multimodal theory. A two-stage experimental study was conducted in a primary school in Southwestern China employing Design-Based Research (DBR) methodology. Results indicated that, compared to conventional teaching models, the MEI model significantly improved students' CT skills, with especially notable impacts on higher-order thinking aspects such as abstraction, algorithms, and evaluation. The study also revealed that the model exerts a significant "protective effect" in maintaining students' attitudes toward CT. This research provides a theoretically grounded and empirically validated framework for deepening students' CT cultivation in ER courses.

TI Multi-agent and multi-modal robotics-facilitated learning for Python
   programming and self-regulated learning
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence in education; Intelligent agent; Robotics for
   education; Adaptive educational systems
ID COMPLETION
AB This study introduces RobotPython, a software-based system with virtual robot assistants designed to support self-regulated learning (SRL)-based Python learning activities for programming novices in an undergraduate non-computer science context. RobotPython includes two virtual robot assistants: the Coding Scaffolding Guidance Assistant and the Flowchart Reflection Assistant, which guide students to learn Python in the performance and self-reflection phases of SRL respectively. Both groups received SRL-based instruction; the key difference was that the experimental group was supported by RobotPython, whereas the control group was supported by teaching assistants (TAs). The 22 students in the experimental group, who used RobotPython as an aid to instruction, achieved significantly higher scores in programming concepts and coding than the 28 students in the control group. The impact of RobotPython on SRL abilities was nuanced: the effectiveness of RobotPython for goal-setting, help-seeking, and self-evaluation was moderated by students' baseline abilities (e.g., task strategies and time management), rather than showing a uniform improvement across all subscales. These results suggest that RobotPython-supported SRL-based instruction is associated with higher programming concept understanding and coding performance, while its impact on SRL abilities is conditional upon students' existing characteristics. They also reveal that programming concept understanding mediates the relationship between SRL abilities and coding performance.

TI Educational robots for student creativity development: Research trends
   and evidence from topic modeling, meta-analysis, and rule mining
SO EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational robots; Creativity; BERTopic; Bayesian meta-analysis;
   Associate rule mining
AB With the increasing adoption of educational robots (ERs) to support creativity development, a comprehensive understanding of their research landscape, empirical effectiveness, and instructional conditions becomes necessary. This study addresses this need by proposing a three-stage analytical framework that involves topic modeling, meta-analysis, and rule mining. First, a BERTopic modeling approach was applied to identify four major research topics, including STEAM motivation and gamified project-based learning, creative coding and narrative play in early childhood, pedagogies for creative and computational thinking, and creative engineering and physical computing, with a growing emphasis on narrative and constructionist approaches, especially in early childhood education. Second, a Bayesian meta-analysis was utilized to identify a moderate overall effect size (Mean = 0.600), with subgroup analyses demonstrating that effect sizes varied significantly across experimental design factors such as subject domain, age group, learning duration, setting, instructional strategy, and measurement issue, where studies focusing on programming education, preschool and high school learners, and guided learning yielded the strongest effects. Finally, an associate rule mining approach was used to identify consistent patterns linking skill modeling, robot-as-tool roles, and mixed instructional strategies with positive creativity outcomes. Findings of this study contribute to both research and practice by enhancing researchers' and instructors' understanding of ER research trends and practical effectiveness in promoting creativity, with actionable instructional design recommendations being provided to optimize ER-based creativity interventions.

TI ABSTRACT REASONING, OTHER KINDS OF REASONING AND ACADEMIC PERFORMANCE IN
   UNIVERSITY STUDENTS
SO ENSAYOS-REVISTA DE LA FACULTAD DE EDUCACION DE ALBACETE
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Abstract reasoning; academic performance; Intelligence; Cognitive
   development
ID INTELLIGENCE; FLUID; MOTIVATION
AB The literature relates abstract Reasoning to academic achievement. The aim of this research is to check this relationship in a University student's population. To this aim, we used a quantitative, cross-sectional and correlational study design. 1161 students aged between 18 and 28 years participated in the research. The figurative analogies test was used to measure abstract Reasoning. The average grade of the Bachelor grades and the grade of the SENESCYT university access exam were used to identify academic performance. As a general conclusion, there is no significant relationship between university access exam and disciplinary grades. If the access exam is indeed a criterion for University access, it should be a predictor of the academic performance. Similarly, the very weak relationship between the average Bachelor degree grades and the AR levels (given the level of Cognitive Development expected in professionals) is worrying. This study should serve for the generation and redesign of educational public policies.

TI STRENGTHS AND WEAKNESSES IN EDUCATIONAL PROCESSES FROM TEACHER'S
   PERCEPTION FOR CREATING INCLUSIVES

LA Spanish
DT Article
DE educational process; school assessment; facilitators; weaknesses;
   improvement; inclusive education
ID STUDENTS
AB This study analyses the strengths and weaknesses of educational processes in three public primary schools from the perspective of teachers, with the aim of developing inclusive practices. An evaluative research design was conducted with a sample of 42 teachers. The Educational Process dimension of the ACADI Guide was used as the assessment instrument. Overall, the results revealed strengths in the categories related to the organization of tutorial action, respect for learning styles, and the organization of teaching. The categories that were positively rated by the schools but still require improvement were respect for students' individual learning paces and characteristics. Regarding weaknesses, specific indicators were identified in each educational institution. The conclusions highlight differences among the educational processes of the schools and emphasize the importance of school self-evaluation in responding appropriately to the particular challenges faced by each institution.

   SPORT EDUCATION

LA Spanish
DT Article
DE physical education; social justice; inclusion; pedagogical models
ID PHYSICAL-EDUCATION
AB The voice of people with disabilities have traditionally been marginalized within the field of research. This study presents a pedagogical experience aimed at amplifying the voices of students with intellectual disabilities during a Sport Education season. To this end, the content, rules, and game dynamics were purposefully negotiated. TI PROCESS OF IMPLEMENTING SUCCESSFUL EDUCATIONAL ACTIONS IN THE LEARNING
   COMMUNITIES OF ANDALUSIA
SO ENSAYOS-REVISTA DE LA FACULTAD DE EDUCACION DE ALBACETE
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Participatory development; community education; cultural transformation;
   social transformation; organizational change
ID INTERACTIVE GROUPS
AB The Learning Communities project aims to transform educational centers by seeking to improve coexistence and inclusion, reduce absenteeism, and enhance student academic performance through Successful Educational Actions. The objective of this study is to determine which of these Actions are present in schools, as well as the strategies employed to implement them. TI ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND DEEP LEARNING: THE ROLE OF COGNITIVE
   FRICTION IN HIGHER EDUCATION
SO ENSAYOS-REVISTA DE LA FACULTAD DE EDUCACION DE ALBACETE
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; deep learning; cognitive friction; critical
   thinking; higher education
ID FRAMEWORK
AB The rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence is transforming learning processes across higher education. Tools capable of producing text, synthesizing information, or solving complex problems may enhance students' immediate performance on a wide range of academic tasks; however, they also raise important pedagogical concerns. The purpose of this article is to examine how the use of generative artificial intelligence may influence the cognitive processes that underlie deep learning. Drawing on the literature on desirable difficulties, the generation effect, cognitive externalization, and critical thinking, the paper analyses the potential risk of conflating fluency with comprehension in AI-mediated learning environments. In addition, the concept of cognitive friction is proposed as an interpretive framework for exploring the conditions that promote students' cognitive engagement in learning. Finally, the article outlines pedagogical principles for integrating these technologies into higher education in ways that support-rather than replace-the cognitive processes essential for meaningful learning.

TI LEARNING THROUGH MEMORY. BEREAVEMENT AND GRIEF IN CHILDHOOD: AN
   INTERVENTION PROPOSAL
SO ENSAYOS-REVISTA DE LA FACULTAD DE EDUCACION DE ALBACETE
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Childhood bereavement; childhood grief; intergenerationality; social and
   emotional education; school nursing
ID SCHOOL; TEACHERS; CHILDREN; METAANALYSIS; HEALTH; DEATH
AB Childhood bereavement requires early educational responses that integrate emotional support, affective regulation, and community-based accompaniment. The aim of this study is to design an intervention for Early Childhood and Primary Education that combines social and emotional learning, an intergenerational approach, and collaboration between education and nursing. The methodology adopts a mixed quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design using the Emotion Regulation Checklist (ERC) and a systematic observation rubric to assess participation, emotional expression, listening, group climate, and symbolic processing of loss. The intervention is organised into four sessions: naming loss, expressing and symbolising, caring and regulating, and remembering and sharing, incorporating narrative, artistic, and intergenerational mediation activities. Expected results include improved emotional regulation, greater pupil participation, and a safer, more empathetic relational climate. Overall, the proposal reinforces the need to address bereavement as a transversal educational content, integrating it into the school's everyday curriculum to foster emotional literacy, resilience, and community care from early childhood, ensuring that loss becomes a shared opportunity for growth rather than an unspoken taboo.

TI EDUCATIONAL ADMINISTRATION IN THE FACE OF INCLUSION OF STUDENTS WITH
   DIABETES: TEACHERS' PERSPECTIVES

LA English
DT Article
DE inclusive education; Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus; educational policy
ID SCHOOL; HEALTH; PERCEPTIONS; ADOLESCENTS; CHILDREN
AB This article aims to highlight the reality of educational administration from teachers' perspectives, focusing on students with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, to develop proposals that enhance inclusive educational processes. The proposals are based on research exploring the biographical narratives of two teachers working with such children. Over five years, six cases of families seeking to enrol their children aged 3-6 in schools in Segovia, Spain, were studied. This qualitative research, with a biographical-narrative design, involved in-depth interviews with these teachers. In the absence of national and regional regulations for the educational needs of children with Type 1 DM, the study proposes: (1) promoting collaboration between educational and healthcare administrations; (2) training educational communities in regulations and inclusive practices; (3) creating regulations for school nurses in public schools; and (4) developing care policies to assist families with the disease.

TI Digital mediation of environmental data and IoT-enabled bioenergy
   education: a perspective on microbial fuel cells in academic contexts
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital literacy; environmental communication; IoT; microbial fuel
   cells; renewable energy; sustainability education
AB The rapid expansion of digital technologies in environmental surveillance has opened new pathways for incorporating data competency, clean energy solutions, and sustainable practices into academic contexts. Although microbial fuel cells (MFCs) present a promising avenue for hands-on learning in bioenergy systems, their application in teaching remains limited. TI A new framework for coping human resource management analysis for
   workplace incivility in higher educational institutions
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education; human resource management; internal marketing;
   qualitative methods; workplace incivility
ID WORK; DEPRESSION; STUDENTS; ANXIETY; STRESS; FUTURE
AB Disrespectful behavior within the workplace is a pervasive issue with consequential implications. In South Asian context, workplace incivility, encompassing incivility, abuse, and harassment, persists as a prevalent yet underreported predicament, notably within academic institutions. Therefore, the primary goal of this study is to thoroughly understand the phenomenon of workplace incivility experienced by faculty members in Pakistan (a South Asian country), including examining its multifaceted consequences and exploring a framework of coping strategies employed by participants in dealing with such adversities to mitigate such issues in higher educational institutions. In this study, the researcher employs a qualitative inquiry and utilizes a descriptive phenomenological method to vividly portray the experiences of faculty members of higher educational institutions subjected to various forms of workplace incivility. Using snowball sampling technique, 21 faculty members of higher educational institutions were interviewed giving detailed accounts of their encounters with workplace incivility. The transcripts from the participant's interviews were analyzed using a phenomenological method through Atlas.ti software elucidated four themes and 21 subthemes. The findings were discussed through Social Network Theory for comprehending and exploring disrespect within Pakistan's higher educational institutions. The study implications, limitations, and future study directions are discussed to put the overall discussion into perspective.

TI Well-being and mental health in university students: a cross-sectional
   group comparison in the context of a campus sustainability strategy
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE eating behavior; emotional overeating; emotional undereating;
   environmental intervention; higher education; negative affectivity;
   psychological well-being; university students
ID STRESS
AB University campuses can serve as environments that promote environmental stewardship through the restoration of green areas, energy and water management, and waste handling. These changes, in turn, may influence students' mental health and well-being. The present study aimed to determine differences in psychological well-being, stress, anxiety, depression, and eating behavior between a group of students assessed before the implementation of a university sustainability strategy and another group assessed after the implementation of the strategy. A comparative design with two independent cross-sectional samples was employed, including one group assessed before the implementation of the campus sustainability strategy (June 2023 = 168) and another group assessed after its implementation (November 2024 = 189). Psychological well-being was assessed using the Ryff Psychological Well-Being Scale, negative affectivity using the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale (DASS-21), and eating behavior using the Adult Eating Behavior Questionnaire (AEBQ). The sustainability strategy included comprehensive environmental actions on campus, such as improvements to green areas, lighting, drinking fountains, cafeterias, gardens, and waste management. Students evaluated following the implementation reported higher psychological well-being scores and lower stress, anxiety, and depression scores, as well as significant reductions in emotional overeating, emotional undereating, and food fussiness. The observed group differences suggest that campus sustainability strategies may be associated with more favorable mental health and eating behavior profiles, although the design does not allow causal conclusions regarding intervention effectiveness.

TI Prevalence of AI chatbot usage and factors associated with AI dependency
   among medical faculty undergraduate students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic self-efficacy; academic stress; AI dependency; artificial
   intelligence; ChatGPT; generative AI; higher education; medical students
ID CHATGPT
AB Background/objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) Chatbots have benefited students in many ways but several issues have arisen with regards to ethical aspects and students' critical thinking skills. This study aims to provide insights to the prevalence and frequency of AI Chatbot usage among Faculty of Medicine, Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (FPER UKM) undergraduate students, and explore the behavioral and psychological factors associated with AI Chatbot use and dependency. Methods: This study employed a cross-sectional design. An online survey involving 300 undergraduate students from FPER UKM consisting of medical, nursing and emergency medicine courses was conducted using questionnaires that were adapted and screened from the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale (BFAS) and other literature. All items were rated on a five-point Likert scale with an inclusion of four open-ended questions at the end of the questionnaire for participants to give their opinion on AI chatbot usage. Two main factors contributing to AI dependency, which are academic stress and academic self-efficacy, were measured using the same scale. Data analysis of the collected responses was then done via bivariable correlation and multivariable regression using SPSS version 29. Results: Our study included 300 students in FPER UKM which mainly consisted of Malaysian students with only 4 of them being non-Malaysian. It was found that the prevalence of AI Chatbot usage among all undergraduate courses to be 100%. Most of the respondents used AI tools for one to three hours per week with the main purpose of studying or revision. The factors most strongly associated with AI dependency score was weekly usage of more than four hours (p < 0.001, beta = 0.301), followed by academic stress (p = 0.001, beta = 0.188). The final multiple regression model was significantly associated with AI Chatbot dependency (p < 0.001) with R-2 of 0.182. Conclusion: All undergraduate students have used AI Chatbot previously with its main benefit on studying and revision. AI Chatbot dependency is significantly associated with duration of AI Chatbot usage and level of academic stress. Further studies are warranted to classify dependency on AI Chatbot and explore other potential correlates related to over-reliance on AI Chatbot.

TI Development and evaluation of a rating scale to assess the quality of
   individualized education plans
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE inclusion; individualized education plans; quality of IEPs; rating
   scale; special educational needs
ID IEPS; CHILDREN; NUMBER; INDEX; ALPHA; GOALS
AB Individualized education plans (IEPs) are widely used in educational settings, particularly in schools, to guide education for students with special educational needs. These plans aim to tailor instruction to students' individual needs ensuring that they receive appropriate support in general or special education classrooms. Their quality seems to be linked to outcomes of instruction, but systematic research on the quality of individualized education plans is lacking. Hence, the aim of this study was to develop and evaluate a rating scale to assess the quality of IEPs that can be used in future research. The resulting R-IEP-scale assesses the quality of IEP parts as well as their coherence. To analyze the psychometric properties of this scale, we used ratings by six raters of N = 99 IEPs. The analysis focused on an exploratory factor analysis, item analyses and the analysis of inter-rater reliability. Results indicated that a one-dimensional structure of the R-IEP-scale showed good internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = .95) as well as appropriate item means (.47-.57) and homogeneity (.69). The inter-rater reliability of the scale was adequate [rWG = .60-.68; ICC(2) = .74-.85], so that the R-IEP-scale can be considered as being valid and reliable. Implications and limitations of the study are discussed.

TI Operationalizing Education for Sustainable Development in higher
   education language learning: a case study of a Chinese
   German-as-a-Foreign-Language textbook
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Education for Sustainable Development; foreign language education;
   German-as-a-Foreign-Language; higher education; textbook analysis
AB Introduction As Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) gain prominence in global education, increasing attention has been paid to how sustainability is made pedagogically usable in teaching materials within the framework of Education for Sustainable Development (ESD), particularly in language textbooks. While sustainability-oriented textbook research has often focused on the inclusion of SDG-related themes, less attention has been paid to how such themes are selected, discursively framed and pedagogically developed. Systematic data-based studies of German-as-a-Foreign-Language (GFL) textbooks remain scarce. This study examines how ESD is operationalized in Meilenstein (volume 3), an intermediate-level GFL textbook newly published and used in Chinese universities.Methods Drawing on Content Analysis and discursive categories informed by Critical Discourse Analysis within an ESD-based coding framework, the study analyzed 248 sustainability-related segments, generating 1,984 coded instances across eight analytical categories in the content, discursive and pedagogical layers. Inter-coder agreement reached Cohen's kappa = 0.93.Results The findings show that sustainability is explicitly represented in the textbook, yet unevenly distributed across SDGs and sustainability dimensions. SDG 13 (Climate Action) functions as the primary anchor and environmental sustainability dominating over social and economic dimensions. Discursively, sustainability is framed predominantly through collective agency and solution-oriented perspectives. Pedagogically, sustainability is translated into competence-oriented learning opportunities that support learner participation and strategic engagement.Discussion By showing how thematic selection, discursive positioning and task design jointly shape the operationalization of ESD in a higher education language textbook, the study contributes a replicable analytical approach and provides case-based evidence of how ESD implementation may take shape in higher education language textbooks, while acknowledging the limits of a single-textbook design.

TI Teaching reform and innovation awareness as a mediator in AIGC adoption
   among vocational information technology teachers: an extended TAM study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adoption intention; AIGC; artificial intelligence-generated content;
   information technology teachers; perceived ease of use; perceived
   usefulness; TAM; teaching reform and innovation awareness
ID ACCEPTANCE MODEL; BEHAVIOR
AB Introduction Artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) is increasingly influencing educational practice, but its effective adoption in vocational education depends not only on teachers' perceptions of the technology itself but also on their awareness of teaching reform and pedagogical innovation.Methods Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), this study developed an extended model to examine how perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEU), and teaching reform and innovation awareness (TRIA) influence AIGC adoption intention (AAI) among vocational information technology teachers. Data were collected from 122 valid questionnaire responses from teachers in 18 vocational colleges. Exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, and bootstrap mediation analysis were used.Results The results show that PU has a significant direct positive effect on AAI, whereas PEU does not directly predict AAI. TRIA significantly predicts AAI and significantly mediates the relationship between PEU and AAI. However, the mediating effect of TRIA between PU and AAI is not statistically significant.Discussion These findings suggest a dual mechanism of AIGC adoption among vocational information technology teachers. PU directly drives adoption intention, whereas PEU influences adoption intention mainly through teachers' awareness of teaching reform and innovation. The study extends TAM by highlighting the pedagogical innovation mechanism underlying AIGC adoption in vocational education and provides practical implications for teacher professional development and institutional support.

TI Project-based language learning: impact among engineering college
   students in rural south Tamil Nadu, India
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE autonomy learning; creativity; product development; project-based
   learning (PBL); student-centric approach
AB The Indian education system consistently analyzes the strengths and weaknesses of students through examinations, with an emphasis on rote learning, text memorizing, and marks earned. These assessments are considered indicators of students' credibility but are not directly associated with practical, critical, or creative knowledge. To address this gap, a student-centered project-based learning (PBL) method was implemented to create a dynamic classroom setup to motivate the learners to solve real-life problems. In this study, a descriptive research design and convenient sampling methods were used, involving 109 first-year engineering students grouped into teams of 5-7 members. Students were tasked with completing two minor projects at the elementary level: a language worksheet and art from waste. Then, the students were assigned two major projects: a skit and model presentation. In the model presentation, students investigated and responded to a problem, a challenge, or a complex question by offering creative solutions. Survey responses from students proved that PBL was highly motivating; the students enjoyed the projects and considered them an edutainment forum, which stimulated their creativity (t-21.553, p < 0.01) in terms of language development (t-17.462, p < 0.01) and product development.

TI Strategic interactional sequencing in Sanskrit epic dialogue as a model
   for communicative language training in ELE
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE communicative competence; communicative outcomes; English language
   teaching (ELT); interactional patterning; discourse organisation
AB Recent work in English Language Teaching emphasises communicative competence beyond grammatical accuracy, yet existing pedagogical models often under-theorise how communication emerges through discourse. This study investigates how interactional patterns in dialogue support the achievement of broader communicative goals. Using qualitative analysis of selected narrative dialogues from classical Sanskrit literature, the study examines how conversational structures unfold across turns rather than through isolated linguistic acts. The results show that interactional patterning organises conversation, guiding coherence, turn-taking, and goal attainment. These findings suggest that communicative outcomes arise from the sequential organisation of interaction rather than from individual language functions. By abstracting from narrative examples to general interactional organisation, the study proposes a transferable framework for understanding spoken communication. This framework advances English Language Teaching by highlighting the role of discourse structure in developing communicative competence and shifting attention from isolated language forms to the patterns of interaction that make communication effective.

TI Culinary Skills of Visually Impaired People and Associated Factors: A
   Cross-Sectional Study
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE visual impairment; culinary skills; cooking autonomy; public health
   nutrition; activities of daily living
ID COOKING SKILLS; MEAL PREPARATION; FOOD; CONSUMPTION; IMPACT
AB Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the culinary skills (CS) of visually impaired (VI) individuals and identify barriers to their culinary autonomy. Design: Cross-sectional study. Setting: Benjamin Constant Institute, an educational institution for the VI students, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Participants: One-hundred and twenty-one adults with VI, aged between 19 and 77 years. Main Outcome Measures: Sociodemographic, economic, and clinical data, and data related to skills and barriers to culinary practice were collected through interviews conducted at the Benjamin Constant Institute. Levels of CS were assessed using an adapted Brazilian Culinary Skills and Healthy Eating Questionnaire (composed of the following scales: Availability and Accessibility of Fruits and Vegetables Index, Culinary Attitude, Culinary Behavior, Culinary Self-Efficacy, and Fresh Produce Consumption Self-Efficacy). Analysis: Descriptive and inferential statistics, including logistic regression, were applied to evaluate associations between CS levels and sociodemographic variables. Results: Of the participants, 78.5% exhibited medium CS, and 21.5% had high CS. Barriers such as difficulty following recipes, using household measures, and preparing fried foods were commonly reported. Black participants were more likely to demonstrate high CS compared with others (odds ratio, 4.41; 95% confidence interval, 1.30-16.51). Braille users were less likely to achieve high CS (odds ratio, 0.28; 95% confidence interval, 0.05-1.00). Conclusions and Implications: Most visually impaired participants demonstrated medium CS, with substantial barriers limiting culinary autonomy.

TI Attributes of Thriving School Gardens in the US
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE school gardens; nutrition education; program implementation;
   sustainability
ID RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED-TRIAL; NUTRITION; PROGRAM; SCIENCE; CURRICULUM;
   RESOURCES; KNOWLEDGE; EDUCATION; BARRIERS
AB Objective: Identify attributes of thriving school gardens and provide recommendations to improve school garden sustainability. Design: Cross-sectional survey administered nationally. Participants: Three hundred and sixty-four school administrators, teachers, and garden coordinators. Main Outcome: Characteristics that predict thriving school gardens measured by a sustainability survey. Analysis: Logistic regression analyses were used to identify which factors predicted the odds of having a thriving school garden. All models were adjusted for Title I status, school classification, and garden age with corrections for multiple comparisons. Statistical significance criterion: P <= 0.05. Results: Each additional subject and grade taught increased the odds to thrive by 21% and 22% (P < 0.001 and P < 0.01, respectively). Schools' odds of having a thriving garden increased 4 times with >= 6 garden workdays (P = 0.05), 7 times with >= 26 annual volunteers (P = 0.02), 9 times with an annual budget > $1,000 (P < 0.001), and 42 times with higher administrative support (P < 0.001). Conclusions and Implications: Administrative support and budget remain integral to garden sustainability, along with volunteer support and garden workdays. School gardens will benefit from fostering administrative support, strategic use of volunteers, increasing classroom use, and developing a sustainable budget. More research is needed to support paid garden staff and garden training for teachers.

AB Objective: To examine the effects of an individualized dietary counseling program informed by health literacy theory in a pilot study of Chinese patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Methods: Randomized controlled trial. Sixty adult hospitalized patients with stage 1-4 nondialysisdependent CKD, mean age 36.6 & sect;12.3 years, were randomly assigned to the intervention group that received a 3-month individualized dietary counseling or the control group receiving enhanced usual care, with outcomes assessed at baseline (T0), discharge (T1), 1 month (T2), and 3 months (T3). However, there was no significant difference in adherence to recommended nutrients intake, as assessed by 24-hour dietary recall, between the 2 groups at T2 and T3. Conclusions and Implications: This health literacy-informed program offers promise for promoting the well-being of Chinese patients with CKD, although confirmation in fully powered trials is recommended before

TI Perceived Childhood Food Insecurity is Associated with Decreased Adult
   Intuitive Eating
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE intuitive eating; food insecurity; food security; child nutrition
ID HEALTH INDICATORS; US ADULTS; QUALITY; WOMEN
AB Objective: To assess the relationship between adult intuitive eating and perceived food security during childhood. Methods: A survey was conducted consisting of the Intuitive Eating Scale-2 and the 6-item short form of the US Household Food Security Module modified to assess perceived food security status in participants aged 0-17 years. Student, faculty, and staff participants (n = 331) were primarily White, women, and aged 18-24 years. Analyses included descriptive statistics, Mann-Whitney U tests, and Kendall's Tau-b correlations. Results: Overall, perceived childhood food insecurity was negatively correlated with adult intuitive eating (Tb =-0.1, P = 0.03) and body-food choice congruence (Tb =-0.1, P = 0.03). When stratified by gender, among women, perceived childhood food insecurity was negatively correlated with adult intuitive eating (Tb =-0.1, P = 0.04). Conclusions and Implications: Perceived childhood food insecurity and adult intuitive eating warrant further exploration to identify those who may benefit from intuitive eating education.

TI Diabetes Nutrition Education and A Food Security Resource for American
   Indian and Alaska Native Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Pilot and
   Feasibility Randomized Controlled Trial
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE American Indian and Alaska Native; food security; diabetes nutrition
   education
ID TRADITIONAL FOODS; INSECURITY; COMMUNITIES; DISPARITIES; PREVENTION;
   PROJECT
AB Objective: To evaluate the feasibility and effects of the What Can I Eat? (CIE) Healthy Choices for American Indians and Alaska Native (AI/AN) Adults with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) curriculum augmented by a food security resource. Methods: A 3-arm pilot randomized controlled trial (n = 67) was conducted at an urban AI/AN clinic with adults with T2D. The groups were as follows: (1) WCIE and food security resource, (2) WCIE alone, or (3) food security resource alone. Feasibility outcomes were collected throughout the study. Baseline and 3-month assessments included sociodemographic, clinical, dietary (24-hour recall), food security, and nutrition behavior measures. Data were analyzed using linear mixed models. Results: Feasibility outcomes were strong: 90% class attendance, 93% retention, > 99% data completeness, and high satisfaction. Randomization and recruitment were successful. Trends suggest improved self-efficacy for healthy eating (0 = 0.3-0.6, P < 0.05) and use of the American Diabetes Association Diabetes Plate (0 = 0.7-1.0, P< 0.05). Conclusions and Implications: What Can I Eat? Healthy Choices for American Indians and Alaska Natives With Type 2 Diabetes is feasible and may enhance healthy eating and self-efficacy among AI/AN adults with T2D.

TI Primary Grocery Shopping Location is Associated With Vegetable
   Consumption in Underserved Communities
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE food shopping; fruit and vegetable intake; food security; food retail
ID LOW-INCOME; FOOD ENVIRONMENT; UNITED-STATES; HEALTHY FOOD; STORE TYPE;
   FRUIT; ACCESS; DIET; AVAILABILITY; PERCEPTIONS
AB Objective: This paper characterizes the relationship between primary grocery shopping location (i.e., primary store type) and food security status, fruit and vegetable consumption, and perceptions of the food environment. Methods: Survey data from shoppers in predominantly lower-income urban areas were analyzed to identify associations with primary store type (supermarket, supercenter, buying club, or small grocery store). Results: Among respondents (n = 698), most reported a supermarket as their primary store type (67.5%). There were no associations between primary store type and food security or fruit consumption, but vegetable intake was higher for small grocery store (2.00 times/d) and supermarket customers (1.82 times/d) compared with supercenter shoppers (1.52 times/d, P = 0.006 and 0.04, respectively). Small stores were also rated as having more affordable produce than supermarkets (P < 0.001), and perceived affordability was associated with higher vegetable intake (P = 0.009). Conclusions and Implications: Understanding shoppers' perceptions of food stores may help identify targets for improving diet.
